blocks.text: A 78-year-old man is admitted after his third fall in four months. He takes fourteen regular medicines, his standing systolic blood pressure drops markedly on getting up, and he has been taking a sedative every night for years. No single drug was prescribed carelessly, yet together they are doing him harm. Deprescribing is the skill of reversing this safely, and adherence is why some patients take none of what we prescribe.

blocks.markdown: **Polypharmacy** means taking many medicines; it is often defined as five or more, but the number matters less than whether each medicine is justified. **Appropriate polypharmacy** is where every medicine is evidence-based, the combination has been reviewed and the patient understands and agrees with it. **Problematic polypharmacy** is where medicines are not benefiting the patient, are unsafe in combination, or are no longer aligned with the patient's goals. Older adults are at greatest risk because of multimorbidity, reduced renal function, altered pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, and increased sensitivity to sedation and anticholinergic effects.

blocks.title: Deprescribing
blocks.text: Deprescribing is the planned, supervised process of reducing or stopping medicines that are no longer beneficial or are causing harm, to reduce harm and improve outcomes, guided by the patient's goals, preferences and circumstances. It is not simply stopping medicines to cut costs or numbers.

rows: Gradual supervised reduction; address insomnia causes
First-generation antihistamine used regularly (for sleep or itch)
Strong anticholinergic effects: confusion, retention, constipation
Stop or substitute a non-sedating option
Anticholinergic bladder drug alongside a cholinesterase inhibitor
Review glycaemic target; choose a safer alternative
Regular NSAID with renal impairment, heart failure or anticoagulant
Proton pump inhibitor without an ongoing indication
Review the indication; step down or stop with advice on rebound symptoms
blocks.caption: Illustrative potentially inappropriate medicines. Applicability depends on the individual; check STOPP/START, the BNF and local guidance.

blocks.markdown: **Tools for identifying inappropriate prescribing.** **STOPP** (Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions) lists potentially inappropriate medicines, and **START** (Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment) lists potentially omitted beneficial medicines. The American **Beers criteria** serve a similar purpose. **Anticholinergic burden** scales add up the cumulative anticholinergic load, and drugs that increase falls risk (sedatives, antihypertensives, antipsychotics, antidepressants and others) deserve scrutiny after a fall. These tools prompt review; they are not rules, because every decision must account for the individual patient.

blocks.title: Structured review of an older patient's medicines
blocks.prompt: An 81-year-old woman with a fall last month takes zopiclone nightly (three years), omeprazole (original indication not documented), amlodipine, ramipril, alendronic acid and oxybutynin, and was recently started on donepezil. Review her list for potentially inappropriate and omitted medicines and set priorities.

steps.text: Clarify the indication for each drug and what the patient wants. Zopiclone: insomnia. Omeprazole: no recorded reason. Oxybutynin: urgency. Donepezil: memory loss. Amlodipine and ramipril: blood pressure. Alendronic acid: bone protection.

Flag potential harms. Zopiclone is a sedative that increases falls and confusion in older adults. Oxybutynin is strongly anticholinergic and opposes donepezil, so the two partly cancel and add cognitive risk. Omeprazole without an indication is a candidate for review. Antihypertensives are relevant to the fall if standing blood pressure is low.

Prioritise by harm and benefit: the sedative and the anticholinergic drug address the most direct fall and cognition risks. Keep alendronic acid because fracture prevention is worth more after a fall, with attention to the correct administration. Check standing blood pressure before adjusting antihypertensives.

Change one thing at a time, with a plan. Begin with a gradual, supervised reduction of the hypnotic or review of the oxybutynin and donepezil pair, agree it with the patient, set a review date, and document each decision. Check the BNF and local guidance for tapering.

blocks.answer: Highest-priority targets are the hypnotic and the oxybutynin and donepezil combination; review omeprazole's indication; retain bone protection; alter one drug at a time with patient agreement.

blocks.markdown: **Principles of deprescribing.** The process is a planned sequence, shown below. Start by weighing **time to benefit** against **remaining life expectancy and goals**: a preventive drug whose benefit takes years to appear matters less in someone with limited life expectancy or whose priorities are comfort, while a drug controlling symptoms may be valuable at any age.

items: Obtain a complete list of what the patient actually takes, including over-the-counter and herbal products (see medicines reconciliation).
Identify the indication and current benefit of each medicine, and the patient's goals and preferences.
Assess harm: adverse effects, interactions, burden and falls or cognitive risk.
Prioritise which medicine to stop first, favouring high harm and low benefit.
Stop or taper one medicine at a time, with an agreed plan; reduce gradually where withdrawal or rebound is possible.
Monitor for relapse, withdrawal and adverse effects; be ready to restart if needed.
Document and communicate the decision to the patient, carers, GP and pharmacy.

headers: Why it may need a gradual reduction
rows: Reduce in stages; follow BNF and local guidance
Taper according to drug and duration of use
Avoid abrupt withdrawal in ischaemic heart disease
Taper; specialist advice for prolonged courses
Step down or on-demand use may help
blocks.caption: Examples where gradual withdrawal is usually advisable. Specific schedules must come from the BNF and specialist or local guidance.

blocks.markdown:
**Adherence** is the extent to which a person takes medicines as agreed with the prescriber. It is a shared responsibility: the older word 'compliance' implies obedience and is less helpful. **Non-adherence** may be **unintentional** (forgetting, difficulty opening containers, misunderstanding instructions, cognitive impairment) or **intentional** (the patient decides not to take it, often because of beliefs about the medicine, perceived side effects, cost, or doubt that it is needed). Contributing factors include the patient, the medicine (complex regimens, side effects), the condition (asymptomatic diseases), the healthcare relationship and the system (access and cost). NICE guidance on medicines adherence stresses a non-judgemental conversation and involving the patient in decisions.

A simple objective measure from dispensing records is the **medication possession ratio (MPR)**: days' supply dispensed divided by days in the observation period, usually expressed as a percentage. A threshold of 80% is often used but is a convention, not a biological limit, and dispensing does not prove ingestion.

rows: Link doses to routines, reminders, once-daily regimens
Simplify and rationalise; combination products where suitable
'I do not want to depend on tablets'
Explore the necessity and concerns; shared decision-making
Ask directly; change drug or dose where possible
Cannot open packaging or use an inhaler
Technique check, adapted packaging, community pharmacy support
Prepayment options, delivery, longer prescriptions where appropriate
blocks.caption: Causes of non-adherence and linked strategies.

blocks.latex: \mathrm{MPR} = \frac{\text{days' supply dispensed}}{\text{days in the observation period}} \times 100\%
blocks.caption: A proxy only: dispensed is not the same as taken.

blocks.title: Assessing adherence before escalating therapy
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old man's blood pressure remains above target on three antihypertensives. Pharmacy records show that over the past 280 days he collected his ramipril as seven 28-day supplies. Before adding a fourth drug, assess adherence.

steps.text: Calculate dispensing adherence. Days' supply = 7 x 28 = 196 days. Days in period = 280. MPR = 196 / 280 = 0.70, which is 70%.

Interpret cautiously. A value of 70% suggests he has missed a considerable portion of doses, but it cannot tell us why, or whether the other drugs show the same pattern. Check all three prescriptions.

Explore the reasons without blame: ask open questions about how he takes the tablets, side effects (for example cough), concerns about long-term treatment, and practical barriers. Check for confirmation that the home blood pressure and technique are accurate.
Act on the cause. Address beliefs or side effects, simplify the regimen where possible, agree a plan and review the blood pressure after adherence has improved, before adding another agent.

blocks.answer: MPR is 70%: adherence should be explored and improved before adding a fourth antihypertensive, and the reasons must be understood.

blocks.title: Ask, do not assume
blocks.text: Apparent treatment failure can reflect non-adherence, so ask how the patient actually takes their medicines before escalating. Equally, a patient's decision not to take a medicine is often rational from their perspective and should be explored, not criticised.

points: Problematic polypharmacy exposes older adults to falls, confusion and adverse effects; each medicine needs a current indication and benefit.
STOPP/START and Beers criteria and anticholinergic burden scales help identify potentially inappropriate medicines and omissions, but judgement is individual.
Deprescribing is planned and person-centred: weigh benefit against harm and goals, change one medicine at a time, taper where needed, monitor and document.
Non-adherence may be intentional or unintentional and has patient, medicine, condition and system causes; MPR is a proxy from dispensing data.
Strategies include non-judgemental discussion, shared decisions, simplification, practical aids, and addressing beliefs and side effects.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a potentially inappropriate medicine for an older adult?
questions.explanation: Potentially inappropriate medicines are those whose risks usually outweigh benefits in older people. Sedating anticholinergics are a classic example because older adults are sensitive to their central and peripheral effects.

options.text: A statin continued after a myocardial infarction in a 76-year-old
A first-generation antihistamine taken regularly each night for sleep
An ACE inhibitor for symptomatic heart failure
A bisphosphonate after a low-trauma hip fracture

questions.correctOptionText: A first-generation antihistamine taken regularly each night for sleep

distractorRationale.a: Secondary prevention after a myocardial infarction is usually appropriate.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: first-generation antihistamines are strongly anticholinergic and sedating, increasing confusion and falls in older adults.
distractorRationale.c: An ACE inhibitor has a clear indication in heart failure.
distractorRationale.d: Bone protection after a fragility fracture is generally appropriate.

questions.stem: What does the START tool aim to identify?
questions.explanation: STOPP and START are used together: one flags potentially inappropriate prescribing, the other potential under-treatment. Both support, but do not replace, clinical judgement.

options.text: Medicines that should be stopped because of interactions
Potential prescribing omissions, meaning indicated beneficial medicines that are not prescribed
The correct dose for patients with renal impairment
Patients who are non-adherent

questions.correctOptionText: Potential prescribing omissions, meaning indicated beneficial medicines that are not prescribed

distractorRationale.a: That is the role of STOPP.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: START alerts clinicians to beneficial treatments that may have been omitted.
distractorRationale.c: Dose adjustment guidance comes from the BNF and renal dosing resources.

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate when deprescribing several medicines in a frail older patient?
questions.explanation: Stopping one drug at a time lets you link any relapse, withdrawal or adverse event to the specific change. Prioritisation focuses effort where harm is greatest.

options.text: Stop all unnecessary medicines on the same day for efficiency
Stop only when the patient requests it
Prioritise high-harm, low-benefit medicines and change one at a time with monitoring and a review date
Taper only the newest medicines first

questions.correctOptionText: Prioritise high-harm, low-benefit medicines and change one at a time with monitoring and a review date

distractorRationale.a: Stopping several together makes it impossible to attribute any new problem to one change.
distractorRationale.b: Clinician-led review and shared decision-making are needed; waiting for requests misses harm.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: prioritising by harm and benefit, changing one thing at a time and monitoring allows safe attribution and reversal.
distractorRationale.d: Recency is not a valid reason; priority depends on harm, benefit and goals.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old stopped her statin after reading online that it is dangerous. She says her cholesterol was only 'a bit high' and she feels well. Which describes this and the best response?
questions.explanation: Intentional non-adherence usually reflects the patient's beliefs about necessity and concerns about harm. Exploring and addressing those beliefs is more effective than simply repeating instructions.

options.text: Unintentional non-adherence; provide a dosette box
Intentional non-adherence driven by beliefs; explore her concerns and the necessity of treatment through shared decision-making
Treatment failure; switch to a different statin
Appropriate deprescribing; no action is needed

questions.correctOptionText: Intentional non-adherence driven by beliefs; explore her concerns and the necessity of treatment through shared decision-making

distractorRationale.a: She made a deliberate decision, so it is not unintentional.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a deliberate decision shaped by beliefs and concerns is best addressed by non-judgemental exploration and shared decisions.
distractorRationale.c: The drug did not fail; it was stopped by the patient.
distractorRationale.d: Deprescribing is a planned clinician-supported process, and this decision followed misinformation without a review.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of unintentional non-adherence?
questions.explanation: Unintentional non-adherence arises from forgetfulness, misunderstanding or practical difficulty, and responds to reminders, simplification and support. Intentional non-adherence needs a conversation about beliefs and preferences.

options.text: A patient decides that a tablet is unnecessary
A patient with mild cognitive impairment who cannot remember whether the morning tablets were taken
A patient who avoids a drug because of a fear of dependence
A patient who stops a drug because of cost concerns after weighing alternatives

questions.correctOptionText: A patient with mild cognitive impairment who cannot remember whether the morning tablets were taken

distractorRationale.b: Correct: forgetting or confusion without a deliberate decision is unintentional.
distractorRationale.c: This is a deliberate belief-driven decision.
distractorRationale.d: This is a deliberate decision, although cost barriers need addressing.

questions.stem: True or false: deprescribing means stopping all of an older patient's medicines.
questions.explanation: Deprescribing is the planned, supervised reduction or withdrawal of specific medicines that are no longer beneficial or are causing harm. Beneficial medicines are continued, and decisions follow the patient's goals and preferences.

options.text: True
False

questions.stem: A patient with a long-term condition was dispensed five 28-day supplies of a medicine over a 180-day observation period. Calculate the medication possession ratio as a percentage, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Days' supply dispensed is 5 multiplied by 28, which is 140 days. Dividing by the 180-day period gives 0.778, so the medication possession ratio is about 77.8%, a proxy that should prompt a conversation rather than a conclusion.

questions.stem: Outline the principles you would follow when deprescribing a long-term medicine for an older patient.
questions.explanation: The answer should show a systematic, person-centred sequence: review, weigh, prioritise, change cautiously, monitor and communicate. Single changes and tapering are key safety features.
markingGuide: Obtain a full and accurate medicines list and the patient's goals and preferences
Confirm the indication and the current benefit; consider time to benefit against life expectancy
Weigh harms, including adverse effects, interactions, falls and cognitive risk
Stop or taper one medicine at a time, with gradual reduction where withdrawal or rebound is possible, following BNF or local guidance
Monitor for withdrawal, relapse and adverse effects, and be willing to restart
Shared decision with the patient and carers; document and communicate to GP and pharmacy

questions.stem: An 83-year-old man takes glibenclamide, regular naproxen for knee pain, ramipril, furosemide and amitriptyline for neuropathic pain. He has had two hypoglycaemic admissions this year and his eGFR has fallen. Identify the medicines of concern with the risk for each, and describe how you would approach deprescribing.
questions.explanation: Good answers identify the high-risk combinations and prioritise by harm. The NSAID combined with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic in declining renal function, and the long-acting sulfonylurea, are the most urgent.
markingGuide: Glibenclamide: long-acting sulfonylurea causing prolonged hypoglycaemia in older adults; review target and switch to a safer agent
Naproxen with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic: increases the risk of acute kidney injury (the so-called triple whammy), and with falling eGFR should usually be stopped and replaced by safer analgesia
Amitriptyline: anticholinergic and sedating, increasing falls and confusion; review the need and consider alternatives
Ramipril and furosemide: review ongoing indication and renal function and monitor
Prioritise highest harm first (hypoglycaemia and NSAID), change one at a time, involve the patient, and monitor glucose, renal function and pain
Document, communicate to the GP and pharmacy, and check doses and alternatives against the BNF

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with asthma has frequent exacerbations and collects his preventer inhaler only occasionally. Discuss possible causes of non-adherence in this case and the strategies you would use.
questions.explanation: A strong answer separates unintentional and intentional causes and links each to a specific strategy. It stresses that technique and beliefs are common and treatable causes of poor control.
markingGuide: Non-judgemental, open conversation to understand his perspective
Unintentional causes: forgetfulness, chaotic routine, poor inhaler technique or difficulty using the device
Intentional causes: concern about long-term steroids or dependence, belief that the preventer is unnecessary when well, side effects such as hoarseness
Strategies: check and teach inhaler technique, consider a different device, link use to a daily routine, reminders, simplify the regimen
Address beliefs by explaining the role of the preventer in avoiding exacerbations, and agree a written asthma plan
Involve community pharmacy and follow up; check dispensing records as a proxy while recognising their limits
